items.followUp: Give two reasons why viruses are considered to lie at the boundary between living and non-living things.

rubric.why: Viruses do not have the cellular organization required for placement in the five kingdoms.
rubric.description: States that viruses are acellular.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that viruses lack cells or cellular structure.

rubric.why: Viruses cannot reproduce independently and depend on host cells.
rubric.description: Explains that viruses reproduce only inside living host cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that reproduction requires a living host cell.

rubric.why: Viruses lack independent metabolic activities characteristic of living organisms.
rubric.description: States that viruses do not carry out metabolism independently.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the absence of independent metabolism or life processes.

rubric.why: Outside a host, viruses can remain inert and may be crystallized, unlike active cellular organisms.
rubric.description: Mentions that viruses are inert outside the host or can be crystallized.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either characteristic.

modelAnswer: Viruses are acellular and have no cellular structure.
They lack independent metabolism and other life activities.
They reproduce only inside living host cells.
Outside a host, they are inert and can be crystallized; therefore, they are not placed in any of the five kingdoms.

items.followUp: Describe how yeast fermentation is used in bread making and name its main products.

rubric.why: Fermentation is an anaerobic process.
rubric.description: Defines fermentation as the breakdown of sugar without oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the process as anaerobic.

rubric.why: Yeast enzymes ferment sugars and release energy.
rubric.description: Identifies yeast fermenting sugar.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning yeast and sugar/glucose as the substrate.

rubric.why: Alcoholic fermentation by yeast produces ethanol.
rubric.description: Names ethanol as a product of yeast fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for ethanol/alcohol.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is another product of alcoholic fermentation and helps dough rise.
rubric.description: Names carbon dioxide as a product or explains its role in raising dough.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for carbon dioxide or its dough-rising effect.

rubric.why: Fermentation has important food and industrial applications.
rubric.description: Gives a useful application of fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid application such as bread making, dairy fermentation, or production of alcohol/biofuel.

modelAnswer: Fermentation is the breakdown of sugar by microorganisms in the absence of oxygen.
Yeast ferments glucose and releases energy.
Alcoholic fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
In bread making, carbon dioxide makes the dough rise.
Fermentation is also used to make yogurt and cheese and to produce alcohol and biofuel.

items.followUp: Name the six major bioelements found in the human body.

rubric.why: Carbon is one of the six major bioelements.
rubric.description: Names carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for at least two correct elements from this group.

rubric.why: Hydrogen is one of the six major bioelements.
rubric.description: Included with the first group.
rubric.how: No separate mark; counted with the first group.

rubric.why: Oxygen is one of the six major bioelements.
rubric.description: Included with the first group.
rubric.how: No separate mark; counted with the first group.

rubric.why: Nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur complete the six major bioelements.
rubric.description: Names at least two of nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for at least two correct elements from this group.

modelAnswer: The six major bioelements in the human body are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur (CHONPS).

items.followUp: Define an organ level of organization and give one example.

rubric.why: A tissue is made of similar cells organized together.
rubric.description: Defines a tissue as a group of similar cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as similar cells grouped together.

rubric.why: Tissue cells work together for a particular function; named tissues are valid examples.
rubric.description: Mentions their shared function or gives a correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the function or at least one valid example, such as epithelial, muscular, nervous or connective tissue.

modelAnswer: The tissue level is a level of organization in which similar cells work together to perform a specific function.
Examples include epithelial, muscular, nervous and connective tissues.

items.followUp: What is induction in scientific reasoning, and how does it differ from deduction?

rubric.why: Deduction begins with a general rule or principle.
rubric.description: States that deduction starts from a general principle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the general starting point.

rubric.why: Deductive reasoning applies the general rule to reach a specific conclusion.
rubric.description: Explains that deduction proceeds from general to specific.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the direction of reasoning or a clear equivalent definition.

modelAnswer: Deduction is reasoning from a general principle or rule to a conclusion about a specific case.
It applies what is generally known to reach a particular conclusion.

items.followUp: Name one disease that mosquitoes can transmit and one local reaction caused by their bite.

rubric.why: Mosquito saliva can cause a local skin reaction.
rubric.description: Names a local effect of a mosquito bite.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for itching, swelling or redness.

rubric.why: Some mosquitoes transmit disease-causing organisms to humans.
rubric.description: Names a disease that mosquitoes can transmit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct mosquito-borne disease.

modelAnswer: A mosquito bite may cause itching, redness and swelling of the skin.
Mosquitoes can also transmit diseases such as malaria, dengue, yellow fever or Zika.

items.followUp: State two structural features shared by mitochondria and chloroplasts.

rubric.why: Both organelles are surrounded by a double membrane.
rubric.description: Identifies their double-membrane structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that both have two membranes.

rubric.why: Both contain their own genetic material and ribosomes and can make some of their own proteins.
rubric.description: Gives a shared feature such as their own DNA or ribosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for at least one valid shared feature.

modelAnswer: Both mitochondria and chloroplasts are surrounded by a double membrane.
Both contain their own DNA and ribosomes and can make some of their own proteins.

items.followUp: What is agriculture, and name one activity involved in it besides growing crops.

rubric.why: Growing crops is a central farming activity.
rubric.description: Mentions the cultivation of crops.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for growing or cultivating crops.

rubric.why: Farming also includes keeping animals and producing useful goods.
rubric.description: Mentions animal rearing or the production of food/useful products.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for rearing animals or a correct purpose of farming.

modelAnswer: Farming is the practice of growing crops and rearing animals.
It provides food and other useful products for people.
